usage: Take the particle 에 (destination/event), never 을 — you go TO the event
Set idiom for the couple having their ceremony; 올리다 (lit. 'raise/offer up') sounds more elevated than 하다
Add 場 (-장, 'place') for the building; 예식장 (禮式場) is the equally common synonym
You receive a 청첩장 (invitation); 초대받다 = 'be invited' in passive
examples: 다음 주에 결혼식이 있어요.
There's a wedding next week.
Simple 있다 existence sentence — note 결혼식이, the subject marker, not 결혼식을
주말마다 결혼식이 많아서 좀 부담돼요.
There are so many weddings every weekend that it's a bit of a financial burden.
마다 = 'every'; weekend weddings + 축의금 are a real money pressure Koreans joke about
부장님 딸 결혼식이라 회사 사람들이 다 같이 갔어요.
It was our manager's daughter's wedding, so everyone from the office went together.
Shows the workplace-obligation register: attending a boss's family wedding is near-mandatory
nuance: 결혼식 is the wedding CEREMONY (식 = 式 'ceremony/rite'), as opposed to 결혼 (結婚, 'tie + marry'), which is the marriage or the act of getting married — so 결혼했어요 means 'I got married,' while 결혼식에 갔어요 means 'I attended a wedding.' That 결혼/결혼식 split is the #1 trap for English speakers, since English 'wedding' blurs both. Compared with the everyday synonym 예식 (禮式, 'ceremony of courtesy'), 결혼식 is the plain default and 예식 sounds slightly more formal/venue-flavored (hence 예식장). The ceremony itself is famously short (30–60 minutes); the socially weighty part is the buffet meal afterward, which your cash gift 축의금 helps cover. Habitual collocations: 결혼식에 가다/참석하다, 결혼식을 올리다, 결혼식장. Take 에 for attendance — 결혼식을 가다 is a common particle error.

mistakes: Don't confuse 결혼식 (the ceremony you attend) with 결혼 (the marriage): '결혼했어요' means YOU got married, so saying it when you only went to a friend's wedding wrongly announces your own marriage. Use 결혼식에 갔어요.
Avoid 결혼식을 가다 — 'go' targets a destination, so the natural particle is 에: 결혼식에 가다. The 을/를 here sounds like you're somehow 'doing' the wedding.
Don't say 결혼식을 하다 for the couple holding it; the idiomatic verb is 올리다 (결혼식을 올리다) or simply 결혼하다.

usage: Particle 에 for attendance; you go to pay respects (조문하다)
장례식장 (場) is the building, often inside a hospital; 빈소 (殯所) is the specific mourning room
參席 'take part'; more formal than 가다, standard in workplace announcements
Said of the bereaved family holding it; drop 식 and use 치르다 ('go through / carry out')
examples: 장례식에 검은 옷을 입고 갔어요.
I wore black clothes to the funeral.
Basic 입고 가다 ('wear and go'); dark, plain clothing is expected
부장님 아버님 장례식이라 부서 사람들이 다 조문하러 갔어요.
It was our manager's father's funeral, so the whole team went to pay respects.
조문하러 가다 = 'go in order to pay condolences'; teaches the -러 purpose ending in a real obligation context
갑작스러운 부고라 장례식장에 바로 달려갔어요.
It was such sudden news that I rushed straight to the funeral hall.
Real-situation register; 달려가다 ('run/rush to') conveys urgency and closeness to the bereaved
nuance: 장례식 is a funeral — 葬 'bury' + 禮 'rite' + 式 'ceremony,' literally the 'burial-rite ceremony.' Distinguish it from the act-focused 장례 (葬禮, the funeral proceedings the family 치르다 'carries out') and from 조문/문상 (弔問/問喪), which is what a GUEST does — paying condolences. So the family 장례를 치르다, while you 장례식에 가서 조문하다. Korean funerals typically run three days at a 장례식장 frequently attached to a hospital, with the 빈소 (殯所, wake room) as the core space. Attending a colleague's or friend's family wake is a heavy social duty; you bring 조의금 in a plain white envelope and wear muted dark clothing. English speakers wrongly carry over 'congratulations'-type warmth — the funeral register is solemn and understated, and bright clothing or cheerful words badly misfire.

mistakes: Don't say or bring anything 축하 (congratulatory): the correct sentiment is 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ('I humbly pray for the deceased's peace') or a quiet word of condolence. 축하 at a funeral is a severe register error.
Don't confuse the white-envelope 조의금 (funeral) with the wedding 축의금; using the wrong word or a colored envelope is a serious faux pas.
Don't mix up 장례식 (the ceremony/event) with 장례 (the family's act of holding it): a guest goes to the 장례식, but it's the family that 장례를 치르다.

usage: Said of the parents throwing it; 하다 is natural here
Coworkers/friends with a baby invite you; implies a gift or cash
The highlight: the baby grabs an object said to foretell its future
答禮 'gift in return'; parents give guests 떡, towels, etc. in thanks
examples: 다음 달에 조카 돌잔치가 있어요.
My niece's first-birthday party is next month.
Simple 있다 sentence; 돌잔치 takes the subject marker 가
돌잔치에서 아기가 돌잡이로 마이크를 잡았어요.
At the doljanchi the baby grabbed the microphone in the doljabi.
에서 marks the location of the action; guests cheer whichever object the baby picks
요즘은 돌잔치를 작게 가족끼리만 하는 집도 많아요.
These days many families hold the doljanchi small, just among relatives.
끼리 = 'among (only)'; reflects the real shift from lavish halls to intimate gatherings
nuance: 돌잔치 = 돌 (native Korean for a baby's first birthday) + 잔치 (native Korean for 'feast/celebration'), so unlike most life-event words here it is NOT Sino-Korean — there's no hanja. 돌 historically marked surviving the dangerous first year when infant mortality was high, which is why it's celebrated rather than treated like an ordinary 생일. Keep that contrast sharp: 돌잔치 is ONLY the first birthday; every later birthday is 생일, and the polite/honorific 생신 is for elders. The signature ritual is 돌잡이, where the baby grabs an object (money, thread, pencil, mic…) believed to predict its future. As a guest you give cash or a baby gift and may receive a 답례품 in return. Watch the spelling: 돌잔치 is one word, not 돌 잔치.

Write it as one word, 돌잔치, not 돌 잔치 with a space; 잔치 ('feast') is fused onto 돌.
Don't call it 첫 번째 생일 파티 as a literal translation of 'first birthday party' — Koreans have the dedicated word 돌잔치, and the calque sounds foreign.

usage: 맞다 = 'greet/meet' a milestone date; 환갑을 맞이하다 is the fuller form
Add 잔치 ('feast'); the traditional celebration party
Use 시 honorific because it concerns an elder
進甲; the year after 환갑, sometimes also marked
examples: 올해 아버지가 환갑이세요.
My father turns 60 this year.
Honorific 이세요 because it's about a parent — never the plain 환갑이에요 for an elder
예전에는 환갑잔치를 크게 했는데 요즘은 잘 안 해요.
People used to hold big 60th banquets, but these days they often don't.
-는데 sets up the past-vs-now contrast; longer lifespans made 60 less momentous
할머니 환갑이라 온 가족이 호텔에서 식사를 했어요.
It was grandmother's 60th, so the whole family had a meal at a hotel.
Real-situation use; shows the modern trend of a family meal/trip replacing a banquet
nuance: 환갑 (還甲, 'return + sexagenary-cycle') literally means the 갑(甲) has come full circle: traditional Korea counts years on a 60-term zodiac cycle (干支), so turning 60 'returns' you to the cycle's start — hence also written 회갑 (回甲, 'revolve + cycle'), the more formal variant. Don't confuse it with the milestone above it, 칠순/고희 (70th, 古稀 'rare since old times'), or with 진갑 (進甲, the 61st). Because life expectancy was once short, reaching 환갑 was a rare achievement worthy of a big 환갑잔치; today, with people routinely living far longer, families more often mark it with a trip or gift than a banquet. Crucial register point: 환갑 always concerns an elder, so use honorifics — 환갑이세요, 환갑을 맞으셨어요 — and pair it with 생신 (not 생일) when naming the birthday itself.

Don't equate 환갑 with simply 'turning 60' in a Western sense — it's tied to the 60-year 干支 cycle and Korean age reckoning, so the cultural weight (and sometimes the exact year) differs.
Don't reach for 생일 when speaking of the elder's day; pair 환갑 with the honorific 생신 (e.g. 환갑 생신).

usage: 받다 implies a soft obligation to attend or send 축의금
Sent as a KakaoTalk link; now the default, bundling a map and account number
돌리다 ('send around') = casually handing them to friends and coworkers
文句 'phrasing'; the formal text announcing the couple and date
examples: 어제 청첩장을 받았어요.
I received a wedding invitation yesterday.
Basic 받다 sentence; 청첩장 takes 을 as the object
친구가 청첩장 주려고 일부러 만나자고 했어요.
My friend asked to meet up on purpose just to give me the invitation.
-(으)려고 = 'in order to'; handing a paper 청첩장 in person is a courteous gesture
모바일 청첩장에 계좌번호랑 오시는 길이 다 들어 있더라고요.
The mobile invitation had the bank account number and directions all included.
-더라고요 reports a fresh discovery; reflects how digital invites bundle 축의금 transfer info
nuance: 청첩장 (請牒狀) breaks down as 請 'request/invite' + 牒 'official note' + 狀 'document/letter' — a 'letter requesting your presence,' specifically for a WEDDING. Keep it apart from the general 초대장 (招待狀, any invitation card to a party/event): every 청첩장 is a 초대장, but you only call it 청첩장 for a wedding. Increasingly it arrives as a 모바일 청첩장, a KakaoTalk link that bundles a map, schedule, and the couple's bank account number for transferring 축의금. Receiving one carries a quiet obligation: you're expected either to attend or to send the cash gift, and ignoring a close friend's or coworker's 청첩장 can genuinely strain the relationship. Habitual verbs: 청첩장을 주다/받다/돌리다. The hanja is opaque even to many Koreans, so just learn it as a fixed word.

Don't treat a received 청첩장 as optional info — from a close friend or coworker it's a soft social obligation; silence (no attendance and no 축의금) can damage the relationship.
Don't say 청첩장을 보내다 only for paper — these days 청첩장을 보내다 most often means sending the KakaoTalk 모바일 청첩장 link, so don't picture an envelope by default.

usage: 내다 ('hand in / pay') is the standard verb at the 접수처 (reception desk)
보내다 = transfer it to their account when you can't attend
封套 'envelope'; a white envelope you sign your name on at the desk
Common baseline amounts; closer relationships and elders give more
examples: 축의금으로 5만 원을 냈어요.
I gave 50,000 won as the gift.
(으)로 = 'as/by means of'; 5만 원 is the common baseline amount
접수처에서 봉투에 이름 적고 축의금을 냈어요.
I wrote my name on the envelope at the reception desk and handed in the gift.
You sign so the couple can record who gave what — teaches the desk routine
결혼식에 못 가서 축의금만 계좌로 보냈어요.
I couldn't make the wedding, so I just sent the gift to their account.
Real situation; -만 ('only') + 계좌로 ('by account') shows transfer is fully acceptable
nuance: 축의금 (祝儀金) = 祝 'congratulate' + 儀 'ceremony/propriety' + 金 'money' — literally 'money for a congratulatory ceremony,' the cash you give at HAPPY events, above all weddings. Its exact mirror image is 조의금 (弔儀金, 'condolence-ceremony money') for funerals: same 儀金 ending, opposite first character (祝 'congratulate' vs 弔 'mourn'), and opposite occasions — confusing the two, or reusing the wrong envelope, is a real and embarrassing error. You place 축의금 in a WHITE envelope, sign it, and hand it in at the 접수처 (reception desk) so the couple can record who gave it. Amounts start around 50,000 won and rise with closeness, traditionally in odd denominations (5/7/10만). The English word 'gift' misleads here — this is specifically cash, not a wrapped present, and a 선물 (a physical gift) is a different thing you generally don't substitute.

Don't give even-numbered amounts like 60,000 or 80,000 won; odd numbers (50,000 / 70,000 / 100,000) are customary, as even amounts traditionally suggest 'splitting.'
Don't translate it as a 선물 ('gift/present') — 축의금 is specifically cash in an envelope; bringing a wrapped object instead can look like you missed the custom.

usage: 내다 ('hand in') at the 장례식장 reception desk
Plain undecorated white envelope, often with 부의 written on it
전하다 ('convey/deliver') sounds respectful and appropriately solemn
賻儀金; used interchangeably with 조의금, and 부의 is what you write on the envelope
examples: 조의금을 냈어요.
I gave condolence money.
Basic 내다 sentence; the solemn counterpart to 축의금을 내다
조의금 봉투에는 보통 '부의'라고 써요.
On the condolence envelope you usually write '부의.'
Teaches the fixed envelope wording, unlike a wedding envelope
멀어서 못 가고 조의금만 동료 편에 보냈어요.
I couldn't go because it was far, so I sent the condolence money with a coworker.
편에 = 'by way of (a person)'; sending it with someone attending is common when you can't go
nuance: 조의금 (弔儀金) = 弔 'mourn/condole' + 儀 'ceremony/propriety' + 金 'money,' the cash given to a bereaved family — the exact dark twin of 축의금 (祝儀金), which swaps in 祝 'congratulate.' The freely interchangeable synonym is 부의금 (賻儀金, 賻 = 'goods given to help with a funeral'), and confusingly the word you actually write on the envelope is usually 부의 or 조의, not 조의금. It goes in a PLAIN WHITE, undecorated envelope handed in at the 장례식장 reception desk, and like 축의금 it's a near-obligatory courtesy for a coworker's family funeral. Because the occasion is solemn, every cue stays understated — no color, no flourish, quiet delivery (전하다). The cardinal English-speaker error is treating any envelope of money as interchangeable; the 祝/弔 distinction and the white envelope are non-negotiable.

usage: Standard verb; particle 을 for the trip you take, 에 for the destination
go and come back from a honeymoon
다녀오다 = 'go and return'; implies the round trip is complete
Add 地 (-지, 'place/land'); e.g. 하와이, 발리, 몰디브
신혼 + 집; the place the couple sets up after marrying
examples: 신혼여행은 어디로 가요?
Where are you going for your honeymoon?
어디로 ('to where') with directional 로; a natural question to a couple
신혼여행으로 발리에 갔다 왔어요.
We went to Bali for our honeymoon.
(으)로 = 'as/for'; Southeast Asian beach resorts are typical 신혼여행지
결혼식 끝나고 바로 신혼여행 다녀와서 집들이를 했어요.
Right after the wedding we went on the honeymoon and then held a housewarming.
Real timeline chaining 결혼식 → 신혼여행 → 집들이, three life-event words in sequence
nuance: 신혼여행 (新婚旅行) = 新 'new' + 婚 'marriage' + 旅行 'travel,' literally the 'new-marriage trip,' i.e. the honeymoon taken right after the 결혼식. usage: 者 'person'; your engaged partner, gender-neutral (no separate male/female word)
반지 = 'ring'; the ring exchanged at engagement
破婚 'break + marriage'; the antonym verb worth knowing
examples: 저희 언니가 약혼했어요.
My older sister got engaged.
약혼하다 as a plain past-tense announcement; the most natural way to report it
약혼자랑 같이 상견례를 준비하고 있어요.
I'm preparing the family meeting together with my fiancé.
랑 = casual 'with'; links naturally to 상견례, the families' first meal
요즘은 약혼식을 따로 안 하고 바로 결혼 준비하는 사람도 많아요.

Real-situation contrast; reflects that formal 약혼식 ceremonies are fading
nuance: 약혼 (約婚) = 約 'promise/pledge' + 婚 'marriage,' literally 'pledging to marry' — the formal engagement, with verb 약혼하다 and partner 약혼자 (約婚者, gender-neutral, so no fiancé/fiancée split to memorize). english: formal meeting of the two families (before marriage)
usage: Said of the two families formally meeting
場所 'place'; usually a quiet, refined restaurant
兩家 'both houses'; the people 상견례 brings together
examples: 다음 주에 상견례가 있어요.
The family meeting is next week.
Simple 있다 sentence; 상견례 takes the subject marker 가
상견례는 조용한 한정식집에서 했어요.
We held the family meeting at a quiet Korean set-menu restaurant.
에서 marks the location of the event; calm upscale restaurants are the norm
상견례 때 너무 긴장돼서 말을 거의 못 했어요.

때 = 'at the time of'; conveys the genuinely formal, tense register of the occasion
nuance: 상견례 (相見禮) = 相 'mutually' + 見 'see/meet' + 禮 'rite/courtesy,' literally 'the courtesy of meeting one another' — specifically the formal first meeting of the two families (양가, 兩家) before a wedding, usually over a meal. Don't generalize it: despite the literal 'mutual meeting,' it does NOT mean any first introduction between strangers — that's just 첫 만남 or 인사. It also isn't 맞선/소개팅 (a matchmaking date between the would-be couple themselves); 상견례 is the PARENTS being introduced once marriage is essentially decided. usage: Said of the host throwing the party
Particle 에 for the event; you attend as a guest
Classic choices: 휴지 (toilet paper) and 세제 (detergent)
The host inviting friends over to the new place
examples: 주말에 집들이가 있어요.
There's a housewarming this weekend.
Basic 있다 sentence; 집들이 takes the subject marker 가
집들이에 갈 때 보통 휴지나 세제를 사 가요.

사 가다 = 'buy and bring'; these gifts carry traditional good-luck meaning
이사하고 친구들 불러서 집들이를 했는데 분위기가 정말 좋았어요.

Real situation; -는데 links the setup to the warm, casual atmosphere of the event

usage: 받다 ('receive'); often arrives via KakaoTalk or a workplace message
전하다 ('convey') sounds appropriately solemn and respectful
The text giving the deceased's name, 빈소, and funeral times
오다 ('come') as an intransitive arrival; used when one is received
examples: 부고를 받았어요.
I received a death notice.
Basic 받다 sentence; note the solemn register the word carries
부고 문자에 장례식장 위치가 적혀 있었어요.
The death-notice text had the funeral hall's location written on it.
적혀 있다 = 'is written (and remains so)'; the message bundles 빈소 location and visiting hours
부고를 듣고 바로 조의금을 준비해서 조문하러 갔어요.
On hearing of the death I prepared condolence money right away and went to pay respects.
Real timeline -고 ('and then'); a 부고 prompts 조의금 and a visit if you're close
nuance: 부고 (訃告) = 訃 'announcement of a death' + 告 'tell/notify,' literally 'notifying of a death' — the formal notice that someone has died, not the funeral itself. Distinguish it sharply from 장례식 (葬禮式, the funeral ceremony) and 빈소 (殯所, the wake room): you first RECEIVE a 부고, which then leads you to attend the 장례식 at the 빈소. The near-synonym 부음 (訃音, 'news of a death') means the same message but sounds more literary; 부고 is the everyday word, today usually circulated as a 부고 문자 listing the deceased, the 빈소, and visiting times. In a workplace, getting a colleague's family 부고 effectively signals that attending and giving 조의금 is expected. Both word and tone are solemn — the English habit of a quick 'thanks for letting me know' reply misfires; respond soberly with condolences, never an emoji or light remark.
